name: a(n) is the minimum size of a subset of Z/pZ with at least 2 elements and no unique sum, where p is the n-th odd prime.
comment: For a subset A of Z/pZ, an element g of A + A is called a unique sum of A if there is exactly one pair {a, b} of elements of A, a = b allowed, with a + b = g, and A has no unique sum if no element of A + A is a unique sum. For odd p this is equivalent to every element of A + A having at least 3 representations as an ordered sum a + b with a, b in A: a single pair {a, b} yields one ordered sum when a = b and two when a != b, and two different pairs {a, a}, {b, b} cannot yield the same sum since doubling is injective in Z/pZ for odd p. The minimum in the name is denoted m(p) in the literature.
Ben Green's "100 Open Problems" includes the problem of estimating m(p) as Problem 27 and credits the question to Andrew Granville and Swastik Kopparty.
The odd primes are the natural index set: in Z/2Z the only subset with at least 2 elements is {0, 1}, where 0 + 1 = 1 has just 2 ordered representations, so no such subset exists for p = 2.
link: B. Bedert, On unique sums in Abelian groups, Combinatorica, 44 (2024), 269-298; also arXiv:2303.15134 [math.CO], 2023.
T. Łuczak and T. Schoen, On a problem of Konyagin, Acta Arith., 134 (2008), 101-109.
E. G. Straus, Differences of residues (mod p), J. Number Theory, 8 (1976), 40-42.
Mark Watson, Unique sums notes (notes on Bedert's paper, with a machine-checked proposition).
formula: a(n) >= w(p)*log(p) for some function w(p) tending to infinity with p, where p is the n-th odd prime; proved by Bedert (2024).
a(n) <= C*(log(p))^2 for some constant C; proved by Bedert (2024), and also follows from Łuczak and Schoen (2008), Theorem 2, together with Straus (1976).
example: a(2) = 4: for p = 5 the set {0, 1, 2, 3} works, since the ordered representation counts of the sums 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 (mod 5) are 3, 3, 3, 4, 3 respectively, e.g., 3 = 0+3 = 1+2 = 2+1 = 3+0; so a(2) <= 4. Checking all ten 3-element subsets of Z/5Z shows none works, so a(2) = 4.
